title: Comparative Advantage: Why Trade Pays Even When You Are Worse at Everything
topic: kinh tế học: lợi thế so sánh
summary: Ricardo's four numbers about English cloth and Portuguese wine still explain why countries trade, who gains, and why the losers of trade matter more than the old textbooks admitted.
body:
Imagine a lawyer who also types faster than anyone in her office. She could do her own typing, and she would do it better than the assistant she pays. Yet almost every lawyer like her hires an assistant anyway. Why? Because every hour she spends typing is an hour she is not spending on legal work that earns far more. The assistant is worse at typing than she is, and much worse at law, but the arrangement makes both of them better off.

That small office scene holds one of the most powerful and most misunderstood ideas in economics: **comparative advantage**. It explains why countries trade even when one of them is better at making almost everything, why a rich nation still imports goods it could produce itself, and why "they are more efficient than us at everything, so we cannot compete" is usually the wrong way to think about trade. It also explains, when it is stretched too far or applied carelessly, why trade has produced real losers and a political backlash that has reshaped elections across the world.

This article walks through the idea from the beginning: where it came from, how the famous numbers work, what it does and does not promise, how later economists refined it, and where its critics have scored real points.

## Before Ricardo: Adam Smith and absolute advantage

The story usually starts with Adam Smith's *The Wealth of Nations*, published in 1776. Smith attacked mercantilism, the dominant view of his time, which held that a nation grows rich by exporting more than it imports and piling up gold and silver. Smith argued that real wealth is the stream of goods and services people can enjoy, and that the division of labour, not hoarding, is what increases it.

He put the household logic plainly. It is, he wrote, "the maxim of every prudent master of a family, never to attempt to make at home what it will cost him more to make than to buy." The tailor does not make his own shoes; he buys them from the shoemaker. The shoemaker does not make his own clothes; he pays the tailor. Each concentrates on what he does well and trades for the rest. Smith extended this to nations: if a foreign country can supply us with a commodity more cheaply than we can make it ourselves, better to buy it with part of the produce of our own industry, employed in a way in which we have some advantage.

This is the idea of **absolute advantage**. If Scotland is better at making wool and Portugal is better at making wine, Scotland should make wool, Portugal wine, and they should trade. Everyone sees the sense in that.

But absolute advantage leaves an awkward question open. What if one country is better at making *everything*? What if a richer, more technologically advanced country has lower costs in every industry? Does the poorer country have nothing to offer, and does the richer country have no reason to trade? Intuition says yes. The intuition is wrong, and the man who showed why was a stockbroker.

## David Ricardo and the four famous numbers

David Ricardo (1772–1823) was born in London to a family of Sephardic Jewish origin that had come from the Netherlands. He made a fortune as a stockbroker and dealer in government bonds, read Smith's *Wealth of Nations* almost by chance while on holiday, and turned to economics in his late twenties. He later bought a seat in Parliament. His major work, *On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation*, appeared in 1817.

Chapter 7, "On Foreign Trade," contains a short example that has been taught to students for two centuries. Ricardo imagines two countries, England and Portugal, and two goods, cloth and wine. He expresses costs in the amount of labour needed to produce a given quantity of each good in a year:

- England needs the labour of **100 men** to make a certain quantity of cloth, and **120 men** to make a certain quantity of wine.
- Portugal needs **90 men** for that cloth and only **80 men** for that wine.

Look at the numbers carefully. Portugal is better at both. It makes cloth with fewer workers (90 against 100) and wine with fewer workers (80 against 120). In Smith's terms, Portugal has an absolute advantage in everything. So why should Portugal buy anything from England?

Ricardo's answer is that what matters is not absolute cost but **relative** cost: what each country gives up to produce one good instead of the other.

### Thinking in opportunity costs

Take England first. The labour that makes one unit of wine (120 men) could instead make 1.2 units of cloth (since one unit of cloth needs 100 men). So for England, one unit of wine "costs" 1.2 units of cloth. Equivalently, one unit of cloth costs about 0.83 units of wine.

Now Portugal. The labour that makes one unit of wine (80 men) could make about 0.89 units of cloth (80 divided by 90). So for Portugal, one unit of wine costs only 0.89 units of cloth, and one unit of cloth costs 1.125 units of wine.

Put side by side:

- Wine is relatively cheap in Portugal (0.89 cloth per wine) and relatively expensive in England (1.2 cloth per wine).
- Cloth is relatively cheap in England (0.83 wine per cloth) and relatively expensive in Portugal (1.125 wine per cloth).

England, though worse at both, is *less bad* at cloth. Its disadvantage in cloth is small (100 versus 90, about 11 per cent more labour) while its disadvantage in wine is large (120 versus 80, 50 per cent more labour). England has a **comparative advantage** in cloth. Portugal, better at both, is *most* better at wine. It has a comparative advantage in wine.

### Where the gain comes from

Suppose each country makes one unit of each good on its own. England uses 220 workers and gets one cloth and one wine. Portugal uses 170 workers and gets the same. Total world output: two cloth, two wine.

Now let them specialise. England puts all 220 workers into cloth and makes 2.2 units of cloth. Portugal puts all 170 workers into wine and makes 2.125 units of wine. Total world output: 2.2 cloth and 2.125 wine. With exactly the same labour, the two countries together have *more of both goods* than before.

Any trading price between the two countries' internal ratios, say one wine for one cloth, lets both share the gain. England trades one cloth for one wine; at home that wine would have cost it 1.2 cloth. Portugal trades one wine for one cloth; at home that cloth would have cost it 1.125 wine. Each gets the imported good more cheaply than it could make it.

This is the core result: **trade based on comparative advantage can make both sides better off even when one side is more productive at everything.** What determines the pattern of trade is not who is best in absolute terms but who has the lowest opportunity cost.

### A footnote on authorship

Ricardo's name is permanently attached to the idea, but historians of economics have long argued about priority. Robert Torrens stated a version of it in *An Essay on the External Corn Trade* in 1815, and James Mill, Ricardo's friend and editor-in-spirit, is sometimes credited with shaping the chapter. Some scholars have also argued that the four numbers are widely misread, and that Ricardo meant them differently from how textbooks present them. None of this changes the logic, but it is a useful reminder that ideas often emerge from conversations rather than single minds.

## Why the idea is so slippery

Paul Samuelson, one of the twentieth century's most influential economists, told a story about this. The mathematician Stanislaw Ulam once challenged him to name a single proposition in the social sciences that was both true and non-trivial. Samuelson could not answer at the time. Years later, he said the answer was comparative advantage: that it is logically true need not be argued before a mathematician, and that it is not trivial is shown by the thousands of important and intelligent people who have never been able to grasp it, or to believe it after it was explained to them.

Why is it so hard to absorb? Several reasons stand out.

1. **We think in absolute terms.** In daily life we compare people and firms by who is "better." Comparative advantage asks a different question: better *relative to what else you could be doing*.
2. **The gains are diffuse, the losses are concentrated.** Cheaper imported wine helps millions of English drinkers a little. English wine producers who lose their market lose a lot. The losers know exactly who they are; the winners rarely notice.
3. **It feels like a zero-sum contest.** News headlines speak of countries "winning" or "losing" at trade, as if a trade surplus were a score. In Ricardo's model, both sides gain, and there is no scoreboard.
4. **It is counterintuitive about the less productive side.** People find it easy to accept that a poor country benefits from trading with a rich one. They find it harder to accept the reverse: that a rich, productive country also benefits from importing from a less productive one.

The lawyer and the typist show the last point well. The lawyer is better at typing, but her opportunity cost of typing is enormous: every hour of typing is an hour of law not done. The typist's opportunity cost of typing is low. Specialisation by comparative advantage frees the lawyer to do more law and gives the typist a job. Both gain.

## The everyday version: opportunity cost everywhere

Comparative advantage is not only about nations. It describes almost any division of labour.

- **In a household**, one partner may be better at both cooking and handling the paperwork, but if their edge is larger in paperwork, the couple saves time when that partner does the paperwork and the other cooks.
- **In a team project**, the strongest member should not do every task. They should take the tasks where their edge over others is greatest and leave the rest, even if they could do those faster too.
- **In a company**, outsourcing payroll or cleaning to specialists is often a comparative-advantage decision. The firm might do it competently itself, but its managers' time is better used elsewhere.

There is a lesson here for people who think of themselves as "good at everything." Being better at many things is not the same as being best used at all of them. The question to ask is always: *What am I giving up by doing this?*

## How the theory grew after Ricardo

Ricardo's model is deliberately simple: two countries, two goods, labour as the only input, constant costs, no transport costs, and workers who can move freely between industries within a country but not across borders. Economists spent the next two centuries relaxing these assumptions to see what survives.

### Heckscher–Ohlin: why do relative costs differ?

Ricardo took the differences in labour productivity as given. He did not explain why Portugal was relatively good at wine. In the early twentieth century, two Swedish economists, Eli Heckscher (in a 1919 article) and his student Bertil Ohlin (in *Interregional and International Trade*, 1933), offered an answer based on **factor endowments**.

Countries differ in what they have plenty of: land, labour, capital, skilled workers, natural resources. A country will tend to export goods that use its abundant factors intensively and import goods that use its scarce factors intensively. A country with lots of farmland exports grain; a country with lots of capital and engineers exports aircraft; a country with a large workforce and lower wages exports clothing and assembled electronics.

Ohlin shared the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1977, partly for this work.

### Stolper–Samuelson: trade creates winners and losers inside a country

The Heckscher–Ohlin framework had an uncomfortable implication, worked out by Wolfgang Stolper and Paul Samuelson in a 1941 paper. If a country opens to trade and the price of the goods it imports falls, the owners of the factor used intensively in those goods lose out, not only relatively but in real terms. In a country rich in capital and poor in low-skilled labour, opening to trade can lower the real wages of low-skilled workers, even as the country as a whole gains.

This is the theorem that makes the politics of trade intelligible. Ricardo's model shows that a nation gains *on the whole*. Stolper–Samuelson shows that the whole is made of groups, and some groups can lose. The textbook answer is that the winners gain enough that they *could* compensate the losers and still come out ahead. Whether they actually do is a political question, not an economic theorem.

### The Leontief paradox

Theories invite testing. In 1953, Wassily Leontief used input–output tables of the US economy to check whether American exports were more capital-intensive than American imports, as Heckscher–Ohlin predicted for the most capital-rich country in the world. He found the opposite: US exports seemed to be relatively labour-intensive. The "Leontief paradox" sparked decades of work. One common response was that American labour was unusually skilled, so the US was effectively exporting human capital. The episode is a good example of how economics refines a theory when the data push back.

### New trade theory: trading the same things

By the 1970s, a puzzle was obvious. Much world trade was not between very different countries swapping very different goods, but between similar rich countries swapping similar goods. Germany sells cars to France, and France sells cars to Germany. Comparative advantage based on different endowments does not explain that well.

Paul Krugman, in work starting with a 1979 paper, showed that **economies of scale** and consumers' love of variety can generate trade even between identical countries. When production gets cheaper the more you make, it pays for each country to specialise in particular varieties or brands and trade them. Which country ends up with which industry can depend partly on history and accident. Krugman received the Nobel prize in 2008 for this analysis of trade patterns and the location of economic activity.

Later work on firms, led by Marc Melitz and others in the 2000s, added that within each industry only the most productive firms export, and that opening to trade raises average productivity by shifting resources toward those firms.

None of these developments overturned comparative advantage. They broadened the list of reasons countries trade and gave a more detailed picture of who wins and who loses.

## What comparative advantage does not say

Because the idea is often used as a slogan, it is worth being precise about its limits.

### It does not say everyone gains

The theorem is about national totals and about potential gains. It is entirely consistent with some people in each country losing, sometimes badly. English winemakers in Ricardo's story lose their industry. The theory says England as a whole is better off, not that every Englishman is.

### It does not say adjustment is painless

Ricardo's workers move instantly from wine to cloth. Real workers do not. A fifty-year-old machine operator in a small town cannot easily become a software developer in a distant city. Skills, housing, family ties and age make labour much less mobile than the model assumes. When adjustment is slow, the losses can last for years or even a generation.

### It does not say the pattern is permanent

Comparative advantage is **dynamic**. South Korea in the 1960s had a comparative advantage in wigs, textiles and other labour-intensive goods. A few decades later it was exporting ships, steel, semiconductors and cars. Its advantage changed because it accumulated capital, education and technology. Comparative advantage describes where a country stands now, not where it must stay.

### It does not settle questions of security or values

A country might choose to keep some domestic production of food, medicines, energy or defence equipment even at a higher cost, as insurance against war, sanctions or supply shocks. The COVID-19 pandemic, when many countries struggled to obtain masks and other medical supplies, made this argument much more prominent. Comparative advantage tells you what the cost of that insurance is; it does not tell you whether the insurance is worth buying.

## The critics: from Hamilton to the "China shock"

Free trade arguments based on Ricardo became central to British policy in the nineteenth century, most famously with the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846, which removed tariffs on imported grain. But there has always been a counter-tradition, and it deserves a fair hearing.

### Infant industries and catching up

In 1791 Alexander Hamilton, the first US Treasury Secretary, presented his *Report on Manufactures* to Congress. He argued that a young country should protect and encourage new industries until they could compete with established foreign rivals. In 1841 the German economist Friedrich List made a similar case in *The National System of Political Economy*, arguing that Britain preached free trade only after it had become industrially dominant behind protective walls.

The core of the **infant industry argument** is that comparative advantage today may reflect history rather than potential. A country with no steel industry will have high steel costs, not because it is incapable of making steel, but because it has not yet learned. Temporary protection might allow learning, scale and skills to develop until the industry becomes competitive.

Modern versions of this argument point to the rapid industrialisation of Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, where governments actively guided investment, protected certain industries for a time, and pushed firms to export. The economist Ha-Joon Chang, in *Kicking Away the Ladder* (2002), argued that today's rich countries mostly used protection when they were developing and then recommended free trade to poorer countries.

Defenders of free trade reply that infant industry protection is hard to do well. Governments find it hard to pick winners, protected industries often lobby to remain protected long after they should have grown up, and many countries that tried protection in the mid-twentieth century, in Latin America and elsewhere, ended up with inefficient industries and slow growth. The East Asian successes, they argue, owed much to export discipline: firms had to compete on world markets, which is very different from simply shutting out imports. The debate remains open, and serious economists sit on both sides of particular cases.

### The China shock

The most influential recent challenge came from empirical work, not theory. In a 2013 paper titled "The China Syndrome," economists David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson studied what happened to American local labour markets after China's rapid rise as an exporter, which accelerated after China joined the World Trade Organization in December 2001.

They found that regions whose industries competed directly with Chinese imports, such as furniture, toys, textiles and some electronics, suffered large and persistent losses in manufacturing employment, lower wages and higher use of disability and unemployment benefits. Workers did not move smoothly to new jobs or new places as the textbook model assumed. A related study by Daron Acemoglu, Autor, Dorn, Hanson and Brendan Price, published in 2016, estimated that rising import competition from China cost the United States roughly 2.0 to 2.4 million jobs between 1999 and 2011, counting effects that spread through supply chains.

This research did not refute comparative advantage. American consumers and many firms benefited from cheaper goods, and other sectors expanded. But it showed that the losses were geographically concentrated, long-lasting and politically explosive, and that the assumption of smooth adjustment had been too optimistic. Many economists who had previously treated the distributional costs of trade as a minor footnote revised their views.

Other researchers have argued that the China shock is sometimes overstated: that automation explains a larger share of manufacturing job losses, that the effects were concentrated in a particular decade and have faded, and that new trade barriers impose their own costs on consumers and on industries that depend on imported parts. This debate, too, is ongoing.

### Trade versus trade policy

It helps to separate two questions that often get mixed together.

- **Does trade create overall gains?** Most economists, across the political spectrum, say yes, and comparative advantage is the main reason.
- **What should be done for those who lose?** Here there is wide disagreement. Options include retraining programmes, wage insurance, relocation help, regional investment, stronger social safety nets, or slowing the pace of liberalisation. Some argue that targeted tariffs are a legitimate tool; others argue they cost far more per job saved than direct support would.

Comparative advantage answers the first question. It is largely silent on the second.

## Comparative advantage in Vietnam's story

Vietnam offers a vivid modern case. After the Đổi Mới reforms launched in 1986, the country gradually opened to trade and foreign investment. In the early years, its comparative advantage lay in agricultural products such as rice, coffee, cashews and seafood, and in labour-intensive manufacturing such as garments and footwear. These reflected Vietnam's endowments: fertile deltas, a tropical climate in parts of the country, and a large, young workforce.

Over time, foreign firms began to build electronics assembly plants, and phones and electronic components became some of the country's largest exports. That shift is comparative advantage in motion. Vietnam did not suddenly become more efficient than everyone at electronics; rather, given its labour costs, its location, its trade agreements and its improving infrastructure, assembling electronics became the use of its resources with the lowest opportunity cost relative to other countries.

The next question for any economy in this position is how to move up the chain, from assembly toward design, components and higher-value services. That is a question about building new comparative advantages through education, infrastructure and institutions, exactly the dynamic process that Ricardo's static model leaves out.

## A worked example you can do on paper

To make the idea stick, try this simple exercise with any two people or two countries.

1. Write down how much time each needs to produce one unit of good A and one unit of good B.
2. For each, calculate the opportunity cost: how many units of B they give up to make one unit of A.
3. Whoever has the lower opportunity cost of A has the comparative advantage in A. The other has the comparative advantage in B.
4. Check that specialising and trading at a price between the two opportunity costs leaves both better off.

Suppose Lan can bake 10 cakes or paint 5 pictures in a day, and Minh can bake 6 cakes or paint 2 pictures. Lan is better at both. But for Lan, one picture costs 2 cakes; for Minh, one picture costs 3 cakes. Lan has the comparative advantage in painting. For Lan, one cake costs 0.5 pictures; for Minh, one cake costs about 0.33 pictures. Minh has the comparative advantage in baking. If Lan paints and Minh bakes, and they trade at a price of, say, 2.5 cakes per picture, both end up with more than they could produce alone.

Once you have done this a couple of times, it becomes clear why the principle applies to so many choices beyond trade: who should do which chores, how a team should split work, which tasks a manager should delegate.

## Five common misconceptions

Because comparative advantage is so often quoted and so rarely worked through, a handful of errors come up again and again. Clearing them away is the quickest way to understand the idea properly.

### "Low wages are an unfair advantage"

People in rich countries often worry that they cannot compete with countries where wages are a fraction of theirs. But wages are not a free-floating advantage; they largely reflect productivity. Workers in rich countries are paid more because, on average, they produce more per hour, thanks to more capital, better technology and more training. Low-wage countries tend to export goods where their productivity gap is smallest, and rich countries export goods where their productivity lead is largest. That is exactly the Ricardian pattern. This does not mean that working conditions or labour rights are irrelevant, only that low wages alone do not mean a rich country "cannot compete."

### "A trade deficit means a country is losing"

In Ricardo's model there is no deficit at all: England pays for wine with cloth. In the real world, a country can import more than it exports for long periods, financed by borrowing or by foreign investment. A deficit may be a sign of problems, or it may simply reflect that foreigners want to invest in a country's assets. Most economists see the overall trade balance as driven mainly by saving and investment decisions, not by whether a country is "good" or "bad" at trade. Bilateral balances, between two particular countries, matter even less.

### "If we import it, we lose those jobs forever"

Specific jobs do disappear, and for the people concerned this is a real loss. But economies also create jobs in exporting industries, in services that use cheaper imported inputs, and in sectors that benefit from consumers having more money left over. The honest statement is that trade changes *which* jobs exist and *where*, often at a painful pace for some places, rather than simply reducing the total.

### "Comparative advantage means a country should only make a few things"

The two-good model implies complete specialisation, but real economies produce thousands of goods, and rising costs as an industry expands usually stop a country from specialising entirely. Most countries end up producing a wide range of goods and trading at the margins.

### "Comparative advantage is just a theory"

It is a logical result: given its assumptions, it must hold. The interesting debates are about which assumptions fit a particular situation, how large the gains are, and how they are shared. That is a debate about application, not about whether the logic works.

## Why it still matters

Two centuries after Ricardo, comparative advantage remains the foundation of how economists think about trade. It explains why trade restrictions usually make a country poorer on the whole, why "they are better than us at everything" is not a reason to stop trading, and why specialisation is the engine of prosperity.

At the same time, the last few decades have made clear that the simple version leaves out much of what matters politically and personally: who loses, how long adjustment takes, which regions bear the costs, and how dependence on others affects security. The most thoughtful defenders of trade today tend to combine Ricardo's insight with serious attention to these distributional and strategic issues. The most thoughtful critics tend to accept that trade creates gains while arguing about how those gains should be shared and how fast economies should be asked to change.

Perhaps the most lasting lesson of comparative advantage is not about countries at all. It is about the habit of asking, every time you choose to do something, what else you could have done with the same time and effort. That habit, more than any trade statistic, is what Ricardo's four numbers teach.
